newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ATHLETICS-MOVE TO CUT COMPULSORY DOPING BANS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-MOVE TO CUT COMPULSORY DOPING BANS.

text.p: International athletics chiefs are to push for a cut in compulsory doping bans from four to two years because the rules are close to collapse and have already been abandoned in Germany because of legal problems.

International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) medical chief Arne Ljungqvist said on Thursday the IAAF would try to persuade its congress to make the changes to its rules at a meeting before the world championships in Athens in August.
The rules need to be changed after it emerged in Germany on Thursday that the country would no longer ban athletes for more than two years because a longer ban is not enforceable under civil law.

The German athletics federation (DLV) will allow former world indoor long jump medallist Susen Tiedtke to return to competition later this month - just two years into a four-year ban for taking steroids.

"We have to have rules that are enforceable by law," Ljungqvist said in an interview. "The proposal for a minimum of two years has the support of federations from Hungary and Russia. We also know there are legal problems in countries like Germany and Spain."
A DLV source added: "We are getting the impression from the IAAF that they are going to accept the two-year bans here (in Germany). We are going to ban for two years from now on."
The sport is now faced with a situation where steroid offenders are facing different sanctions depending on their nationality.
The much-publicised Katrin Krabbe cases in Germany in 1992 and 1993 showed the DLV that four-year bans were considered under German civil law to be too harsh and therefore unacceptable.

In 1995 the IAAF congress voted against a proposal to cut the four-year ban for serious drugs like steroids because of worries it would send the wrong signal to drug cheats. In an emotional debate, Britain was a major opponent to change.
This time the congress may have to ignore the moral aspect and face the practicalities of civil law.

Tiedtke, who married the former American Olympic sprint bronze medallist Joe Greene, tested positive for steroids the day after she won a bronze medal at the world indoor championships in Barcelona in March 1995.

German athletics sources said the IAAF was now looking at the case and its council was expected to allow former East German Tiedtke to compete internationally under its "extraordinary circumstances" rule at a meeting later this month.
Tiedtke has been training hard and if the decision goes her way she would be eligible to compete at the Athens world championships.
German distance runner Martin Bremer, who was also banned for four years in October 1994 for steroid use, is also expected to be allowed to return early with the IAAF's approval.
Ljungqvist refused to comment on the two cases and would not confirm that the IAAF was close to making a final decision.
But athletes serving four-year bans around the world are sure to feel frustrated at the sight of the Germans returning early.
And the IAAF will almost certainly have to change the rules this year to preserve the credibility of its anti-drugs campaign.
